speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: asked the Minister for Communications and Information regarding the recent data leak of more than 800,000 blood donors' personal information from the database of HSA (a) what is the role of the Personal Data Protection Commission in investigating this incident; and (b) whether any review is being done to ascertain whether HSA has acted reasonably in protecting the personal data, including whether the contractual obligations between HSA and its IT vendor reasonably safeguarded the personal information entrusted to these parties.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching
text: asked the Minister for Communications and Information in view of data breaches across public IT systems (a) whether it is justifiable for public agencies to be exempted from Personal Data Protection Act; (b) what recourse do citizens have, other than to complain to agencies or seek civil action; and (c) whether there should be a tangible penalty meted out to these public agencies for public accountability.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: The Senior Minister of State for Health has earlier outlined the review of HSA’s data security policies and practices that is being undertaken.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: As HSA is a Government agency, the Smart Nation and Digital Government Group is also conducting an investigation into the incident.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Ms Irene Quay has asked if it is justifiable that public agencies are exempted from PDPA.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Implicit in the Member’s question is the presumption that public sector agencies are not accountable for their data protection practices or not held to a high standard because the PDPA does not apply to them.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: That is wrong and simply not the case.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Public sector agencies are subject to a different piece of legislation and other regulations.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: In particular, public sector agencies have to comply with the Government Instruction Manuals and the Public Sector (Governance) Act (PSGA).

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Collectively, they have comparable if not higher standards of data protection, compared to PDPA, and similar investigations and enforcement actions are taken against data security breaches.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: I have previously explained in Parliament why we have adopted this approach.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: To reiterate, PDPA does not apply to public agencies because there are fundamental differences in how the public sector operates, which requires a different approach to personal data protection when compared to the private sector.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: In order to enable a whole-of-Government approach to the delivery of public services, personal data has to be managed as a common resource within the public sector.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: The considerations are different in the private sector, as there is no such expectation of a holistic approach to the delivery of commercial services across private organisations.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Citizens have the same recourse for a data breach in the public sector as with PDPA.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Where citizens suspect that their data has been mishandled by a private sector organisation, they can lodge a complaint with PDPC, or with GovTech, if a public sector agency is involved.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: In practice, there are no wrong doors, and the complaint will be directed to the relevant agencies for follow-up.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Affected individuals can also seek mediation or take civil action against the organisation or agency which mishandled the data.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: The Member has asked whether tangible penalties should be imposed on public agencies for public accountability.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Public officers who flout the Government’s data security rules and are found to have misused or disclosed data in an unauthorised manner, could be held criminally liable under PSGA.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: It is not meaningful to impose financial penalties on public sector agencies because the cost of such penalties would ultimately have to be borne by the same public purse.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: The Government has also increased the number and types of internal IT audits to check on agencies’ data access and data protection measures.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: This includes measures and processes related to the collection and protection of citizens’ personal data by public sector agencies, as well as vendors who handle personal data on behalf of the Government.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: While individual agencies are investigating and taking action on the specific incidents, this Committee will undertake a comprehensive review across the public sector and incorporate industry and global best practices to strengthen data security.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: This review will help to ensure that all public sector agencies maintain the highest standards of data governance.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: This is essential to uphold public confidence and deliver a high quality of public service to our citizens through the use of data.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: The work of this Committee will complement our efforts to achieve our Smart Nation vision.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: We will take the supplementary questions for the earlier Parliamentary Questions as well as for these two.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: It was reported that the server was also accessed by several other Internet protocol (IP) addresses.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Is it by foreigners or locals and will we be pursuing any actions on them?

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Do they have the information on the blood donors as well?

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: For those who failed to donate their blood due to illnesses, can this sensitive information be accessed?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: That is still being looked into and when we have a fuller position on this and have more clarity, we will provide those answers.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The first is, I am glad to hear that he confirmed that the private sector vendor Secur Solutions Group is actually governed by the PDPA and that PDPC is looking into their conduct.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: My first question will be, is the PDPC going to wait for the outcome of the HSA investigation and then, follow on from there or is it concurrent?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The second question is, it was mentioned that the Prime Minister has now convened a cross-Government committee chaired by Deputy Prime Minister Teo to look into standards of Government IT security.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Does this confirm that the Government is actually not satisfied and that the standards so far have been wanting in the public sector?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The Minister mentioned that it was not meaningful to fine public agencies because the fine would in the end come from the public purse.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: But can the central Government not operate on the premise that no additional money is going to be provided to public agencies to pay fines and, therefore, the agencies would just have to cope with cuts somewhere else to pay these fines, whether it is from bonuses of Senior Management or whatever it is?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Because there is still an important signalling effect, that the Government is prepared, as an organisation, to abide by the same standards it expects of small businesses.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: The second question is what the establishment of the Public Sector Data Security Review Committee means.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: I think the Member is trying to score a political point here, and I want to make it categorically clear.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: The Government has been working – and that is why I said so in my answer – consistently working and improving data security standards.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: There is a list of things that we have been doing over the years and this has been explained in the House many times in response to the Member's questions and that of many other Members as well.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: The key point here is that, because there have been a series of these incidents in recent times, the Prime Minister and the Government have assessed that we need to take a holistic look again.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: That does not mean that what we have is inadequate or lacking.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: But what it does mean is that we should ensure that we put a total effort to ensure that we leave no stones unturned in ensuring the highest standards are met in the public sector when it comes to data security.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: If there is something that is to be learnt, whether it is from best practices in the private sector or from global companies, that is something we will be very happy to learn from and incorporate in the Government's practices.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, if you fine yourself, you do ask the question, what is the signalling effect there?

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: It is far more important that the signalling effect is that you are taking this issue seriously and holding relevant people accountable.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, that is why, in the way we go about this, the penalties are focused on the individuals, officers, who have made decisions or taken actions which were deemed to be not compliant and, therefore, there are the consequences that I spelt out.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Having said that, when you take action against an organisation in the public sector, the reputational impact on that organisation and leadership is significant.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: I think the Member will concede that that, in itself, is also a major signalling point, because no organisation, public or private, wants to have its reputation tarnished.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Having said that, we are prepared to look at all means to ensure there is clear accountability and ensure that, in the public sector, we have the highest standards of data security.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: That is why this committee has been set up, and we will be open to suggestions.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: If the Member has interesting ideas on this, we would be happy to hear from her.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: The Minister reassured the House that we have the various acts to impose a high standards of responsibility on public agencies.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: However, upon reviewing that, there seems to be a lack of clarity in this Act regarding accountability for data breaches.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: The focus seems to be on misuse of data.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: My second supplementary question is: the Minister informed the House that the public agencies have regular mandatory internal audits in place to ensure public agencies comply with these standards for data protection and security of information and communications technology systems.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: In that case, why are these potential lapses not surfaced during previous internal audit checks?

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Yes, and has the Member also looked at Instruction Manual (IM) 8?

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Because when we look at them holistically, it will be clear that the issues with data, whether it is a breach or misuse, is when I can argue that there is a kind of continuum here.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: But let me assure Members that when you have a breach of data, you have to establish why it occurred.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: If it is because of misuse, there will be a certain set of actions.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: If it is because your systems were not in place, it has to result in a different set of actions to correct the systemic errors.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: If there were certain people accountable for that systemic error, then they have to be held to account as well.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, there is a flow in the way this will proceed in terms of action against Government organisations.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: The second point on regular IT audits, why did they not throw up such issues in the past, I think that is an age-old question.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: You have it in financial audits, you have got quality audits, but you still have incidents.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: This is because it is human beings running the system and, from time to time, it can happen.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: What is important is that when they occur, we learn from these incidents and set them right, and be transparent about what we are doing and how we are going about it.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A question for Senior Minister of State Edwin Tong.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Is the Senior Minister of State able to answer any aspect of my questions?

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Can the Member elaborate on what other aspects have not been answered?

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Dennis Tan's question relates to the circumstances in which the information is placed on the server.
